title: Electromagnetic Energy
lead: Light is a wave, with a wavelength and a frequency whose product is the speed of light, and it is also a stream of photons, each carrying an energy set by its frequency. Traveling and standing waves and the electromagnetic spectrum come first. Then come three observations that classical physics could not explain: blackbody curves, the photoelectric effect and the line spectra of the elements.
objectives: Explain the basic behavior of waves, including travelling waves and standing waves
Describe the wave nature of light
Use appropriate equations to calculate related light-wave properties such as frequency, wavelength, and energy
Distinguish between line and continuous emission spectra
Describe the particle nature of light
summary_html: Light and other forms of electromagnetic radiation move through a vacuum with a constant speed, c, of 2.998 $\times$ 108 m s−1. This radiation shows wavelike behavior, which can be characterized by a frequency, ν, and a wavelength, λ, such that c = λν. Light is an example of a travelling wave. Other important wave phenomena include standing waves, periodic oscillations, and vibrations. Standing waves exhibit quantization, since their wavelengths are limited to discrete integer multiples of some characteristic lengths. Electromagnetic radiation that passes through two closely spaced narrow slits having dimensions roughly similar to the wavelength will show an interference pattern that is a result of constructive and destructive interference of the waves. Electromagnetic radiation also demonstrates properties of particles called photons. The energy of a photon is related to the frequency (or alternatively, the wavelength) of the radiation as E = hν (or $\kE=\frac{hc}{\klam}$), where h is Planck's constant. That light demonstrates both wavelike and particle-like behavior is known as wave-particle duality. All forms of electromagnetic radiation share these properties, although various forms including X-rays, visible light, microwaves, and radio waves interact differently with matter and have very different practical applications. Electromagnetic radiation can be generated by exciting matter to higher energies, such as by heating it. The emitted light can be either continuous (incandescent sources like the sun) or discrete (from specific types of excited atoms). Continuous spectra often have distributions that can be approximated as blackbody radiation at some appropriate temperature. The line spectrum of hydrogen can be obtained by passing the light from an electrified tube of hydrogen gas through a prism. This line spectrum was simple enough that an empirical formula called the Rydberg formula could be derived from the spectrum. Three historically important paradoxes from the late 19th and early 20th centuries that could not be explained within the existing framework of classical mechanics and classical electromagnetism were the blackbody problem, the photoelectric effect, and the discrete spectra of atoms. The resolution of these paradoxes ultimately led to quantum theories that superseded the classical theories.

exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. The three Check Your Learning items carry the book’s own answers from the notes that follow them. Answers to the end-of-chapter exercises come from the book’s key, which covers the odd-numbered items of the chapter’s list; the seven unkeyed items are all numerical and are left out, with no answer computed: fs-idm65612800 (the wavelength of an FM station at 103.1 MHz), fs-idp23451200 (the energy of mercury’s 435.8 nm line), fs-idp158798576 (the frequency, wavelength and color of lithium’s photons), fs-idm74058400 (the frequencies and color of rubidium’s two lines), fs-idp80961152 (the infrared photons that warm a cup of water), fs-idp181189472 (the photons that trip a reptile’s visual signal) and fs-idp156427216 (the Blu-ray laser). The item on the colors of an RGB display is keyed with approximate values the book says may differ, so it is an open answer to compare with. Nothing is taken from another section and nothing is held for one. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: One-dimensional sinusoidal waves show the relationship among wavelength, frequency, and speed. The wave with the shortest wavelength has the highest frequency. Amplitude is one-half the height of the wave from peak to trough.

Portions of the electromagnetic spectrum are shown in order of decreasing frequency and increasing wavelength. (credit “Cosmic ray": modification of work by NASA; credit “PET scan": modification of work by the National Institute of Health; credit “X-ray": modification of work by Dr. Jochen Lengerke; credit “Dental curing": modification of work by the Department of the Navy; credit “Night vision": modification of work by the Department of the Army; credit “Remote": modification of work by Emilian Robert Vicol; credit “Cell phone": modification of work by Brett Jordan; credit “Microwave oven": modification of work by Billy Mabray; credit “AM radio": modification of work by Dave Clausen)
This schematic depicts how amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) can be used to transmit a radio wave.

A vibrating string shows some one-dimensional standing waves. Since the two end points of the string are held fixed, only waves having an integer number of half-wavelengths can form. The points on the string between the end points that are not moving are called the nodes.
Blackbody spectral distribution curves are shown for some representative temperatures.

Photons with low frequencies do not have enough energy to cause electrons to be ejected via the photoelectric effect. For any frequency of light above the threshold frequency, the kinetic energy of an ejected electron will increase linearly with the energy of the incoming photon.

exercises.prompt: One of the frequencies used to transmit and receive cellular telephone signals in the United States is 850 MHz. What is the wavelength in meters of these radio waves?

answer.hint: Divide the speed of light by the frequency, with 850 MHz written as 8.50 × 10⁸ s⁻¹.

exercises.prompt: The microwaves in an oven are of a specific frequency that will heat the water molecules contained in food. (This is why most plastics and glass do not become hot in a microwave oven-they do not contain water molecules.) This frequency is about 3 $\times$ 10<sup>9</sup> Hz. What is the energy of one photon in these microwaves?

answer.hint: The frequency is given, so use E = hν directly.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the threshold energy in kJ/mol of electrons in aluminum, given that the lowest frequency photon for which the photoelectric effect is observed is 9.87 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.

answer.hint: Find the energy of one photon at the threshold frequency with E = hν, then multiply by Avogadro’s number and convert joules to kilojoules.

exercises.prompt: The light produced by a red neon sign is due to the emission of light by excited neon atoms. Qualitatively describe the spectrum produced by passing light from a neon lamp through a prism.

answer.solution: The spectrum consists of colored lines, at least one of which (probably the brightest) is red.

exercises.prompt: FM-95, an FM radio station, broadcasts at a frequency of 9.51 $\times$ 10<sup>7</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (95.1 MHz). What is the wavelength of these radio waves in meters?

answer.hint: Rearrange c = λν to give the wavelength.

exercises.prompt: Light with a wavelength of 614.5 nm looks orange. What is the energy, in joules, per photon of this orange light? What is the energy in eV (1 eV = 1.602 $\times$ 10<sup>−19</sup> J)?

parts.hint: Use E = hc/λ with the wavelength in meters.
Divide the energy in joules by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/eV.

exercises.prompt: A photon of light produced by a surgical laser has an energy of 3.027 $\times$ 10<sup>−19</sup> J. Calculate the frequency and wavelength of the photon. What is the total energy in 1 mole of photons? What is the color of the emitted light?

parts.hint: Divide the energy by Planck’s constant.
Divide the speed of light by the frequency and convert meters to nanometers.
Multiply the energy of one photon by Avogadro’s number.

answer.solution: ν = 4.568 $\times$ 1014 s−1; λ = 656.3 nm; Energy mol−1 = 1.823 $\times$ 105 J mol−1; red

exercises.prompt: The emission spectrum of cesium contains two lines whose frequencies are (a) 3.45 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> Hz and (b) 6.53 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. What are the wavelengths and energies per photon of the two lines? What color are the lines?

parts.hint: Divide the speed of light by the frequency.
Multiply Planck’s constant by the frequency.

answer.solution: (a) λ = 8.69 $\times$ 10−7 m; E = 2.29 $\times$ 10−19 J; (b) λ = 4.59 $\times$ 10−7 m; E = 4.33 $\times$ 10−19 J; The color of (a) is red; (b) is blue.

exercises.prompt: One of the radiographic devices used in a dentist's office emits an X-ray of wavelength 2.090 $\times$ 10<sup>−11</sup> m. What is the energy, in joules, and frequency of this X-ray?

parts.hint: Divide the speed of light by the wavelength.

exercises.prompt: RGB color television and computer displays use cathode ray tubes that produce colors by mixing red, green, and blue light. If we look at the screen with a magnifying glass, we can see individual dots turn on and off as the colors change. Using a spectrum of visible light, determine the approximate wavelength of each of these colors. What is the frequency and energy of a photon of each of these colors?

answer.solution: Red: 660 nm; 4.54 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> Hz; 3.01 $\times$ 10<sup>−19</sup> J. Green: 520 nm; 5.77 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> Hz; 3.82 $\times$ 10<sup>−19</sup> J. Blue: 440 nm; 6.81 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> Hz; 4.51 $\times$ 10<sup>−19</sup> J. Somewhat different numbers are also possible.

exercises.prompt: What is the threshold frequency for sodium metal if a photon with frequency 6.66 $\times$ 10<sup>14</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> ejects an electron with 7.74 $\times$ 10<sup>−20</sup> J kinetic energy? Will the photoelectric effect be observed if sodium is exposed to orange light?

answer.hint: The photon’s energy hν is the threshold energy plus the kinetic energy of the electron; divide the threshold energy by h.
